lines: A team's analytics bill doubles over a few months, while the actual business behind it barely grows at all.
A full month gets spent tuning cluster sizes, and the savings from that month turn out to be almost nothing.
One single query, quietly scanning an entire table over and over for a dashboard nobody's opened since it launched, turns out to be most of that bill.
Worth reasoning through before the reveal settles it.
A whole month of effort went into tuning how big the clusters were. The actual largest line on the bill is something else completely.
Which one is it?
answer: Effort spent is never evidence of where a cost actually sits.
One unwatched query, scanning a full table on every single run, turns into a charge for bytes read that can dwarf anything cluster tuning could ever hope to save.
That whole month of tuning simply went into the wrong category of cost entirely.

lines: A handful of cost categories make up any bill: raw compute, storage, moving data around, individual requests, and software licensing.
Re-expressing each one per unit of whatever the business actually sells makes wildly different designs, and different scales, finally comparable to each other.
And every single number here has to trace back to an actual, dated price someone looked up, never something simply assumed.
Re-sort those same categories purely by their actual share of the total bill, and they almost never come out anywhere close to even.
One of them usually towers over every other category combined.
Spending real effort improving the smaller categories first, before that one dominant category has even been found, is effort spent on the wrong problem.

Three particular shapes show up as that dominant category again and again: bytes read by a query, data crossing between zones that didn't need to, and compute sitting there paid for but doing nothing.
Naming which of those three shapes is actually happening here is the real diagnostic step. A bill essentially never needs five separate fixes. It needs exactly one.
Once that one dominant category is actually named, a specific lever lands directly on it.
That lever doesn't just vaguely help. It shrinks the category by a ratio someone actually measured, with a real saving attached to it, stated per unit of business.

Redraw that exact same ranked picture for a design where data crossing zones happens to be the dominant category instead, and a completely different lever applies: keeping things local, respecting which zone data actually lives in.
Redraw it again for a design where paid-for, idle compute dominates, and the lever changes again: scaling down automatically, or pausing entirely.
Whichever lever gets reached for has to match whichever category is actually dominant. The lever that fixes one of these three does essentially nothing for either of the other two.
That first lever's own saving shrinks the dominant bar convincingly.
Right beside it, though, a second, thinner bar quietly starts growing: a brand new cost that pre-processing the data ahead of time to avoid all that scanning has itself just introduced.
Any lever that successfully lowers one cost can introduce a second cost of its own, and that second cost has to be priced too, not simply ignored.
Pricing a design honestly means pricing it per unit of the actual business, across every one of those categories.
Ranking those categories by actual share finds the one that genuinely dominates, instead of guessing.
A lever gets picked to match that specific dominant category, with its saving stated as an actual measured ratio.
And that lever's own second-order cost gets priced right alongside whatever it saved, not left out of the picture.
One more, to use this for real: months later, with the design itself completely unchanged, one provider cuts their price for moving data between zones sharply.
Does the same ranked picture, run again against that brand new price sheet, still show the exact same category dominating as before?
answer: Not necessarily, and definitely not something to simply assume.
Rankings here are built from actual billed share, and that share moves the instant any one price moves underneath it.

A steep enough cut to whichever category used to dominate can hand the lead over to a category that never changed at all — which is exactly why this gets re-run on fresh numbers, never assumed to still hold from before.
